name: Public speaking course

lead: Public speaking courses and clubs teach you to deliver speeches and take feedback, building confidence and delivery for a more commanding presence.

Repeated practice in front of audiences, with peer or instructor feedback, is the route. Clubs such as Toastmasters International use peer evaluation and impromptu speaking. Studies cited on Wikipedia associate teaching public speaking with greater self-confidence, though direct research on anxiety reduction is limited.

paras: People join a club, school class or commercial course and give speeches regularly over weeks or months.
No harms are documented beyond cost and time.

chain: Repeated practice in front of audiences
angle.text: Repeated practice in front of audiences lowers anxiety and sharpens delivery, so you come across with more confident presence. Confidence gains are reported for such training.

lead: A public speaking course is structured training in delivering speeches to a live audience, offered by clubs, schools and commercial providers. People take them to build the voice, posture, eye contact and calm confidence that make them come across as more composed and magnetic in person, a part of looks that is about presence rather than features.[1]

Courses typically combine prepared speeches, feedback from an evaluator, impromptu speaking drills and coaching on delivery: tone of voice, pace, pauses, volume, body language and positioning, which the classical Roman writer Cicero listed under the canon of delivery.[1] Clubs such as Toastmasters International run peer-evaluated meetings in which members give prepared speeches and impromptu 'Table Topics' talks.[1][2] Commercial programmes such as the Dale Carnegie Course, first taught at a New York YMCA in 1912, teach public speaking alongside self-confidence and human-relations skills.[3]

Fear of public speaking, called glossophobia, is often cited as one of the most common phobias, and the Wikipedia article on the topic says studies associate public speaking training with increased self-confidence.[1]

paras: Public speaking, or oratory, means delivering a speech to a live audience in order to inform, teach or influence it. Modern speeches are usually organised into an introduction, body and conclusion, and the delivery canon of Cicero covers tone of voice, pace, pauses, volume, body language and positioning.[1] Training guidance advises against distracting gestures and recommends working from an outline rather than a full script.[1]
Training formats include clubs, weekly courses, contests and self-paced video and online programmes, which have grown since the 2000s.[1]

Training in speaking goes back to the Sophists of ancient Greece, who taught paying students, and to Roman orators who adapted Greek methods into a full curriculum; Aristotle's Rhetoric (c. 350 BCE) described speaker credibility, emotion and argument as the three persuasive appeals.[1] Demosthenes is said to have practised with pebbles in his mouth, while speaking and running, and rehearsing before a mirror.[1]

Dale Carnegie began teaching public speaking in 1912 at a YMCA in New York, and his course grew into the Dale Carnegie Course; his book How to Win Friends and Influence People followed in 1936.[3] Ralph C. Smedley founded the club that became Toastmasters on 22 October 1924 at the YMCA in Santa Ana, California, and the organisation was incorporated in 1932.[2]

Toastmasters clubs average about 22 members and usually meet weekly or biweekly; meetings consist of prepared speeches with feedback and Table Topics impromptu talks. Its Pathways programme offers paths covering public speaking, interpersonal communication, leadership and confidence, and the organisation reported about 265,000 members in 149 countries in 2025.[2] Its World Championship of Public Speaking began in 1938.[2]
Other programmes include Rostrum in Australia, with over 100 clubs, and Speaking Circles.[1]

Glossophobia is described as possibly primal in origin and related to social anxiety disorder, past public humiliation and stage fright.[1] The Wikipedia article on public speaking says studies link training to increased self-confidence, though it does not name them.[1] Posture and speaking style are also associated in psychology with how confident and open a person appears to others.[4]

No studies found on public speaking courses as an appearance intervention. Related research includes a laboratory study of cardiovascular reactivity during speech tasks, which used public speaking as a stressor, and a 1974 report on a public speaking course for foreign medical graduates.[5][6]

timeline.event: Dale Carnegie begins teaching a public speaking course at a New York YMCA.[3]
Ralph Smedley founds the first Toastmasters club in Santa Ana, California.[2]
